questions.key_step: Noticing that the intersection of the three parallel planes is $(a,b,c)$ and that the intercept-form distance condition is then the locus.
questions.justification: One familiar move: distance of the intercept-form plane from the origin, then renaming (a,b,c) as (x,y,z). No casework or computation. Same demand as the simple direct-formula questions such as 2024-P1-Q12 (L1).

questions.key_step: Translating 'parallel to the plane' into $\vec{AB}\cdot\vec n=0$ and 'parallel to the line' into a parametric point on the line through $A$.
questions.justification: Two short routine sub-calculations (a point on L with AB perpendicular to the normal, and the line from A meeting the plane) chained, no real insight beyond reading the oblique-distance wording. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2), a multi-step vector chain.

questions.key_step: Taking $P=(r,r,r)$ from the three coordinate faces, then solving the distance equation to the slant face and rejecting the extraneous root.
questions.justification: Intercept form and the distance formula in a small chain with one decision (sign choice, rejecting r=3). Nothing unfamiliar. Close to 2024-P1-Q12 (L1) in ideas but with one more stage, so Level 2.

questions.key_step: Foot of the perpendicular is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so $PA=PC=BP$, giving both end points along the line.
questions.justification: Standard foot-of-perpendicular computation followed by moving a fixed length along the line; three routine stages with heavy but mechanical arithmetic and no hidden idea. Similar in demand to 2026-P2-Q7 (L3) but simpler, so Level 2.

questions.key_step: Writing $\left(\frac md\right)^2=(\sum a^2)(\sum a^{-2})$ and bounding it below by $9$.
questions.justification: Intercept-form distance plus one standard inequality (AM-GM/Cauchy-Schwarz) with equality at a=b=c; one well-known trick applied once after a short setup. Numerical format nudges it from 1 up to 2. Comparable to routine questions such as 2024-P1-Q12 (L1) / 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Expressing each altitude as $\frac{3V}{A_i}$ and bounding $(\sum A_i)(\sum \frac{1}{A_i})\ge16$.
questions.justification: A short chain: recall $V=\frac13Ah$, substitute, then one standard inequality (AM-HM); equality case exists. No heavy calculation. Level 2 like other routine multi-step vector/geometry chains, e.g. 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Recognising that the rotated vector is a multiple of $(\vec{OP}\times\hat i)\times\vec{OP}$ (in-plane, perpendicular to $\vec{OP}$) and fixing the sign by the sense of rotation.
questions.justification: Needs the less-practised idea of constructing an in-plane perpendicular with a vector triple product and then settling the sign from 'passing through the positive x-axis'; the arithmetic is short. A vector-construction question with a numerical answer, similar to 2021-P1-Q19 (L3).

questions.key_step: Using $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=0$ to get $\left|\vec c\right|$ and $\vec b\cdot\vec c$ quickly.
questions.justification: Routine chain: angle from dot product, magnitude of a combination using perpendicularity of the cross product, then the angle. No insight beyond standard identities. Level 2, like the multi-step vector chain in 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Applying four standard formulas correctly, especially the oblique distances in (iii) and (iv).
questions.justification: Four independent parts, each a direct standard formula with moderate arithmetic and a slip-prone sign in the plane equation; no hidden idea. Level 2, similar in nature to 2024-P2-Q6 (L1) multi-part checks but with more parts, and 2026-P2-Q7 (L3) upper bound.

questions.key_step: Expanding $\{(n\vec a+\vec b)\times(n\vec b+\vec c)\}\cdot(n\vec c+\vec a)$ and noticing only two triple products survive.
questions.justification: A single familiar move: expand the triple product bilinearly and cancel terms with repeated vectors, then read the determinant form of the triple product. Short and routine; Level 1 as with 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) / 2026-P2-Q4 (L1) style one-trick items.

questions.key_step: Using the diagonal-bisection property to locate $E,F$, then the cross-product area formula.
questions.justification: Straight chain of standard steps: midpoint equations, two vectors, cross product, magnitude. Routine arithmetic and nothing hidden; Level 2 as in 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Computing $V$ and the opposite-edge distance from the three edge vectors at one vertex (or via the cube embedding).
questions.justification: Two standard quantities of a regular tetrahedron computed and divided; the Gram determinant or the cube picture makes it short but a student must set up the skew-line distance correctly. Level 2, below 2023-P1-Q5 (L3) cube skew-line distance maximisation which needs more.

questions.key_step: Expand BAC-CAB, compare coefficients of independent b and c, and bound sin(alpha) by (beta-1)^2+1.
questions.justification: Several routine steps (triple product, coefficient comparison, a.c=1) end with a completing-the-square bound that must be noticed, and there are no options to check. Close to 2021-P1-Q19 (L3), a vector numerical needing a chain of dot-product conditions.

questions.key_step: Reduce the triple cross product to [abc] times a vector, so the product vanishes only when [abc]=0 (excluding the parallel case).
questions.justification: The identity for (axb)x(bxc) is known but the case analysis (zero or parallel) must be done carefully, and a second part asks for an explicit vector product with no options. Placed below 2025-P2-Q12 (L4, coplanarity with parameters) because there is no parameter family to handle.

questions.key_step: Read the angles from the figure (90+beta and 90-beta with z) and dot with v and w to get two equations.
questions.justification: Routine chain: interpret the figure, form two dot-product equations and add them; no real insight beyond angle bookkeeping, but a symbolic answer and a sign slip are possible. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L2), a short vector computation with a couple of standard steps.

questions.key_step: Expand a in the basis b, c, d and read coefficients with triple products; then use coplanarity of the four points.
questions.justification: A textbook two-part proof, but it needs a clean basis argument and the correct sign bookkeeping in the triple products, and the second part needs the right coplanarity expression. Between 2023-P2-Q4 (L1, coplanarity checks) and 2025-P2-Q12 (L4, coplanarity with parameters), so level 3.

questions.key_step: Compute B x C and solve the three component equations.
questions.justification: Cross product followed by a routine 3x3 linear system; no decision beyond matching components, though arithmetic must be careful. Near 2024-P2-Q11 (L0), a direct expression in a basis.

questions.key_step: Equate components and solve the 3x3 linear system.
questions.justification: A direct solution of three linear equations with no concept decision, only arithmetic. Same demand as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0), reading off coefficients in a basis.

questions.key_step: Dot with u to get V.u = 1, then square the equation and use Lagrange's identity for |V x u|^2.
questions.justification: Needs two linked ideas: a dot product to get V.u, then squaring and the identity for |V x u|^2; no options to check. Similar demand to 2021-P1-Q19 (L3), vector numerical from dot-product conditions.

questions.key_step: Spot that x, y, x cross y are independent, then treat the coefficient as a quadratic with three roots.
questions.justification: Two linked ideas (independence of x, y, x cross y; quadratic with three roots is zero) that are standard but must be noticed, with short execution. Below 2025-P2-Q12 (L4) which has a parametric coplanarity.

questions.key_step: Sides are half the sum and half the difference of the diagonals; area is half the magnitude of their cross product.
questions.justification: Two standard formulas, each applied once, with routine arithmetic. Simpler than 2026-P2-Q1 (L2), the vector area question, as no condition has to be decoded.

questions.key_step: Turn the vector equation into a homogeneous 3x3 system and set its determinant to zero.
questions.justification: Routine set-up and determinant, then a cubic that factors with a quadratic; precision matters (the PDF itself slipped) but no real insight. Comparable to 2021-P1-Q7 (L1, consistency of a 3x3 system) plus longer arithmetic, so level 2.

questions.key_step: r = lambda (a x b), then fix lambda from the dot-product condition.
questions.justification: Two familiar steps (cross product, then one scalar equation) with simple arithmetic. Same demand as 2024-P2-Q11 (L0) but with one extra step, so level 1.

questions.key_step: Write the two perpendicularity conditions (altitude from each known vertex is perpendicular to a side through C) and solve.
questions.justification: Two dot-product equations and a 2x2 linear solve, with a small risk of mixing up which side each altitude is perpendicular to. Near 2024-P1-Q12 (L1, orthogonality condition fixes parameters) with a slightly longer chain.

questions.key_step: Turn 'parallel' into the continuous function f1 g2 - f2 g1 and apply IVT from the sign change -5 to 32.
questions.justification: One familiar reformulation (parallel iff 2D cross product vanishes) followed by one IVT sign check; short but the proof format and the link to IVT are mildly non-routine. Nearest anchor 2021-P2-Q3 (IVT/Rolle reasoning, L2).

questions.key_step: Apply AM-GM to the three column sums, then see that all six determinant terms occur in the expanded product of the sums.
questions.justification: The AM-GM step on column sums is not a standard vector manoeuvre, and the student must also handle the absolute value of the determinant; short once seen but the idea is outside the usual coaching pattern. Nearest anchor 2023-P1-Q3 (existence argument, L4) and 2021-P1-Q19 (vector volume, L3).

questions.key_step: Write each bisector unit vector as (u+v)/(2cos(alpha/2)) and use [a x b, b x c, c x a] = [a b c]^2 together with [u+v, v+w, w+u] = 2[u v w].
questions.justification: Two standard textbook results (bisector as sum of unit vectors, triple product of cross products) chained with an expansion of a triple product; long but no hidden trick, with some risk in constants. Nearest anchor 2021-P1-Q19 (vector triple-product chain, L3).

questions.key_step: Notice |b| = |c| so equal angles reduce to a.b = a.c, then substitute y = x + 2z to get (x+z)^2 = 0.
questions.justification: Routine dot-product conditions chained with some algebra; the observation |b|=|c| and the perfect square save a lot, and the sign condition must be used to reject the second solution. Nearest anchor 2025-P2-Q12 (vector conditions in components, L4) is harder; 2024-P1-Q12 (L1) is simpler, so L3 lies between.

questions.key_step: Minimising |r+bs| gives b = -(r.s)/|s|^2, i.e. r+bs is perpendicular to s, and the expression collapses to |r|^2.
questions.justification: Standard minimisation of a quadratic in b followed by a short substitution; two familiar moves with no trap. Nearest anchor 2026-P2-Q1 (dot-product identities for |a+b|, |a-b|, L2).

questions.key_step: Express c as a combination of a and b, take dot products with b, c and d, and solve for the normalised coefficients (which are -1 and 1).
questions.justification: Three dot-product equations in the coplanar combination plus the insight that angle(a,c) is 2pi/3; a moderate chain with normalising lengths where slips are easy. Nearest anchor 2021-P1-Q19 (u.w, v.w conditions with volume, L3).

questions.key_step: Volume gives the height DE = 2, so AE^2 = 16 - 4 = 12 and E is at distance 2 sqrt3 from A on either side along the median line.
questions.justification: Chain of base area, height from volume, right-triangle Pythagoras and a ratio equation with two roots (one with E outside the segment AF), so a student must remember the second solution. Nearest anchors 2026-P2-Q7 (foot of perpendicular and ratio in 3D, L3) and 2025-P1-Q9 (L4).

questions.key_step: With A as origin, dot products a^2/2 between the edge vectors give CE = CF = sqrt7 a/3 and EF = a/sqrt3; then the area of the isosceles triangle.
questions.justification: Three routine length computations from dot products followed by an area formula; many steps but each is standard with no insight needed. Nearest anchor 2026-P2-Q1 (vector lengths and area of a triangle, L2).

questions.key_step: The vector condition gives the circle x^2+y^2=4, and then |PA||PB| = sqrt(25-4x^2) depends on x alone.
questions.justification: Dot product gives a circle, a short simplification gives a one-variable function, and the range of x finishes it; routine with no trap beyond using closed bounds for x. Nearest anchor 2026-P2-Q1 (L2); 2021-P1-Q9 (locus with products of distances, L4) involves heavier computation.

questions.key_step: Use $(\vec{a}-\vec{c})\perp(\vec{b}-\vec{c})$ to split $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2$ (Pythagoras) and read off the combination.
questions.justification: One neat orthogonality idea turned into a short algebraic identity; the given parallelogram condition is a distractor. Comparable to 2026-P2-Q1 (L3) where several vector-length relations are combined; no heavy computation.

questions.key_step: Eliminate $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^2$ using (1),(2) and complete the square with $|\vec{c}|^2=1$.
questions.justification: Routine chained algebra reusing the Q34 identity; the completing-the-square recognition is the only decision. Close to 2026-P2-Q1 (L3), a chain of several length relations, though options make it checkable.

questions.key_step: Use $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}-\vec{c}|=\sqrt{7}$ with $|\vec{c}|=1$ and the triangle inequality to bound $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|$.
questions.justification: Needs the previous two results and a bounding idea (triangle inequality on a derived vector) rather than a direct computation; feasibility of the extremes is easy to skip. Paragraph parts rate high; nearest anchor 2025-P1-Q16 (L4), a vector-conditions chain.

questions.key_step: Cross and dot the given relation with $\vec{p}$ to find $c$ and $\vec{r}$, then evaluate the triple product.
questions.justification: A standard-but-not-trivial technique (solving a vector equation with p x r and p.r given) followed by a 3x3 determinant; three stages with a recognisable trick and distractor options. Comparable to 2025-P1-Q16 (L4) but without its second equation, so one level lower.

questions.key_step: Expand $(\vec{p}\times\vec{q})\times\vec{r}$ by the triple-product identity and substitute the Q37 values.
questions.justification: Direct application of one standard identity with values already found in Q37; routine multi-step substitution, no insight. Nearest anchor 2024-P1-Q16 (L3, direct computations in a paragraph-style item) but lighter.

questions.key_step: Compute $\vec{y}$ from the triple-product identity, evaluate $[\vec{x}\,\vec{y}\,\vec{r}]$ and relate $\frac{1}{6}|\cdot|$ to $|c|$.
questions.justification: Longer chain than Q38 (get y, a 3x3 determinant, recognise tetrahedron vs parallelepiped), and four statements to discriminate, but all steps are routine given Q37-Q38. Anchor 2023-P2-Q4 (L3) for checking several geometric statements on vectors.

questions.key_step: Decode $|\vec{a}+\vec{b}|=1$ into $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-\frac{1}{2}$, then evaluate one dot product.
questions.justification: Two short steps with a standard decoding of a length condition; no casework. Typical routine item, above plain Level 1 because the second dot product has to be chosen and the non-zero denominator checked. Compare 2026-P2-Q1 (L3) which chains more length relations.

questions.key_step: Dot with $\vec{a}$ to get $\mu=2\lambda$, use $|\vec{c}|=1$, and choose the sign by $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}>0$.
questions.justification: Standard solve for coefficients in a plane with one sign subtlety; a few steps without a new idea. Anchor 2024-P2-Q11 (L4, expressing a vector in a basis) is harder because of the triple-product basis, so this sits lower.

questions.key_step: Reduce to a linear optimisation in $x,y$ using $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=0$ and $\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$, with the maximum at $x=1$.
questions.justification: Needs the geometry of the previous parts (angles $120^\circ$, $30^\circ$) and a small optimisation with two-sided bounds; no options to check, but few steps. Rated near 2025-P2-Q12 (L4, no-options vector numerical) yet clearly shorter, so L3.

questions.key_step: Each row needs one or two standard moves; the only care point is checking that jumps of [6x/pi] are not hidden in (B).
questions.justification: Four independent one-to-three-step items (factorisation, jump check, triple product, squaring a vector relation); matching allows elimination and nothing is unfamiliar. Level 2 like the routine vector anchor 2026-P2-Q1 (L2).

questions.key_step: Recognise that equal dot products force d = k(a+b+c), then dot with a and with d to get 3cos^2(alpha)=1+2cos(theta).
questions.justification: A single non-obvious symmetry insight plus an elimination, after which the four rows are one-line evaluations; options make errors easy to spot. A notch above the routine vector matching anchor 2025-P1-Q16 (L2) because the symmetric-axis idea is less drilled.

questions.key_step: Four independent multi-step items; the decisive moves are the plane/parametric intersection in (A), rejecting mu=5 in (C), and folding the integral in (D).
questions.justification: Each of the four rows is a full question in its own right (3-6 stages: skew-line intersection, ITF subtraction formula, vector algebra with an unreal root to reject, and a Dirichlet-kernel integral) with real precision risk, so this is well above the usual short matching item. Placed at the top of the matching anchors, level with the heavy 2026-P1-Q15 (L4) rather than 2026-P1-Q16 (L3).

questions.key_step: Evaluate each row with one standard move: triple product identity, cos(A-B)<=1 bound, and imposing x,y>0 on the intersection of two lines.
questions.justification: Four short independent items each needing one standard idea; (D) needs a little care with the sign of a, and the key is in the options so errors are easy to catch. Equal to the routine matching anchor 2025-P1-Q16 (L2).

questions.key_step: Standard recognitions in each row: n1 x n2 as plane normal, tan^-1 telescoping, half-angle tangent formula, foot of perpendicular.
questions.justification: Four independent two-to-four step items, each using a familiar textbook technique, with the answer list allowing a quick check. Same weight as the routine matching anchor 2025-P1-Q16 (L2).
